Motionary

Motionary is a gesture-controlled online dictionary built with JavaScript. Users can search definitions, pronunciations, synonyms, antonyms, and example sentences, and they can scroll and move between pages with hand gestures picked up by a webcam, so they don’t have to touch a keyboard or mouse.

Motionary: An Event-Driven, Gesture-Controlled Web Encyclopedia for Touchless Student Learning

Sherwin Carbonilla
BSIT – 301i
Jose Rizal University
Mandaluyong City, Philippines
Kenneth Dela Torre
BSIT – 301i
Jose Rizal University
Mandaluyong City, Philippines
Andrei Joaquin Demano
BSIT – 301i
Jose Rizal University
Mandaluyong City, Philippines
Abstract

Web learning tools are usually operated with a mouse, a keyboard, or a touchscreen, and most web apps do not offer touchless navigation. This paper presents Motionary, a student encyclopedia web application built for Jose Rizal University (JRU) that combines a dictionary and thesaurus, a Word of the Day, grammar guides, a slang catalog, and a vocabulary game called Word Catcher with webcam-based hand-gesture navigation. Using a developmental research design, the team built a React single-page application with an Express and SQLite back end and an event-driven gesture pipeline: a MediaPipe hand landmarker detects hand landmarks on the user’s own device, a gesture session stabilizes each pose, and an event bus publishes recognized gestures to subscribers following the Observer pattern. Dictionary lookups pass through a local database, the Free Dictionary API, and Datamuse, with caching, a circuit breaker, and stale-if-error behavior. In the verification reported here, all 162 automated tests in 19 test files passed, the linter reported 0 errors and 0 warnings across 76 files, and the production build succeeded. Contrast ratios computed from the documented color tokens range from 4.93:1 to 13.14:1. Camera video is processed on the device and is never uploaded. Gesture recognition accuracy, response latency, and learning outcomes were not measured in this study and are left to future work with students. The work shows that an event-driven design can add an optional touchless layer to a student learning app while mouse, touch, and keyboard input keep working, and it relates to SDG 4 (Quality Education).

Keywords: Observer pattern MediaPipe hand tracking touchless interaction vocabulary learning web application
162 / 162 TESTS PASSING 0 LINT ERRORS (76 FILES) 4.93:1 – 13.14:1 WCAG AA ON-DEVICE PRIVACY SDG 4 • QUALITY EDUCATION
Section I Introduction ▾

Background and Context

Motionary is a student encyclopedia web app built for Jose Rizal University (JRU) under the tagline “An Encyclopedia made by Students for Students.” It combines a searchable dictionary and thesaurus, a Word of the Day, grammar guides, and a slang catalog with an educational vocabulary game, Word Catcher. It also adds a feature that most web apps do not have: it can be navigated without touching the mouse or keyboard. Using the webcam, it recognizes hand gestures in real time and turns them into navigation and selection actions, while normal mouse, touch, and keyboard input keep working.

Event-driven programming structures software around events that are produced by sources, delivered through a channel or broker, and handled by listeners [1], [2]. The Observer pattern captures one form of this idea: when an object changes state, the objects that depend on it are notified automatically, so the notifying object does not need to know how its observers react [3]. Motionary applies this idea to a camera. A gesture session publishes recognized gestures, and any component, such as navigation, the pointer overlay, or the camera window, can subscribe without knowing how the camera works. The back end also runs on Node.js, which describes itself as an asynchronous event-driven JavaScript runtime [4].

Turning a camera feed into dependable commands raises practical problems. A hand pose seen in a single frame may be accidental, and one gesture can be seen in many consecutive frames. Motionary therefore requires a pose to be held for about 150 ms before it counts and adds a cooldown after each gesture to prevent flicker and repeated jumps. A second problem is dependence on outside services: a dictionary that relies on online sources must keep answering when those sources fail.

Problem Statement

Motionary addresses four needs: (i) vocabulary, grammar, and slang learning should be easy and enjoyable for students; (ii) real-time, on-device computer vision should be demonstrated inside a practical education web app; (iii) touchless navigation should coexist with traditional input rather than replace it; and (iv) the dictionary should keep working during outages of its online sources. Left unaddressed, a touchless layer that fires on every passing hand pose or a dictionary that fails with its data provider would make the app unreliable for the students it is meant to help.

Proposed Solution and Objectives

The proposed solution is the Motionary web app. Its main components are a React single-page application, an Express API, an embedded SQLite database, a MediaPipe-based gesture engine, an event bus, and a small draggable Picture-in-Picture (PiP) camera preview. The expected outcome is a working application whose features are implemented and verified through automated tests, static analysis, a production build, and accessibility checks. The objectives are to (i) make vocabulary, grammar, and slang learning easy and enjoyable; (ii) demonstrate real-time, on-device computer vision inside a practical education web app; (iii) offer touchless navigation that coexists with traditional input methods; and (iv) keep the interface consistent with JRU’s identity (navy, yellow, and gold).

Contributions

This paper makes the following contributions:

  • Technical: an event-driven gesture pipeline in which capture, detection, stabilization, dispatch, response, and data access are decoupled through the Observer pattern, with two interaction modes (hands-free off and on).
  • Practical: a documented implementation with curated content (30 words, 15 slang terms, and 8 grammar topics), the Word Catcher game, and a three-tier word lookup service.
  • Empirical (limited): verification results from 162 automated tests, static analysis, a production build, and contrast ratios computed from the design tokens. No user study is reported.
  • SDG alignment: Motionary relates to SDG 4 (Quality Education) [5] as a learning resource that offers vocabulary, grammar, and slang content and a vocabulary game, with an optional touchless way to use them.
Section II Review of Related Literature ▾

Event-Driven Programming and the Observer Pattern

Hohpe and Woolf catalog messaging patterns for integrating enterprise applications [1], and Luckham treats streams of events in distributed enterprise systems through complex event processing [2]. Gamma et al. describe the Observer pattern at the scale of objects within one program [3]. These sources work at different scales, from enterprise messaging to in-process notification, and Motionary uses the smallest: an in-browser event bus for gesture events. None of them concerns camera input, so how noisy camera frames become discrete events is left to each application. Motionary answers this with a stabilization stage before dispatch.

On-Device Hand Tracking

MediaPipe is a framework for building perception pipelines [6], and MediaPipe Hands is an on-device, real-time solution that predicts a hand skeleton from a single RGB camera [7]. Depth sensors such as the Microsoft Kinect are another route to touchless input [8], and Rautaray and Agrawal survey vision-based hand gesture recognition for human–computer interaction [9]. These works concentrate on sensing and recognition. How recognized poses should be mapped to navigation in a content web app, and how that control should coexist with mouse and keyboard, is left to the application.

Dwell Selection and Unintended Activation

Jacob studied eye-movement-based interaction and described both the Midas Touch problem, in which every look can trigger a command, and the use of dwell time, in which an object is selected when the user keeps looking at it long enough [10]. Motionary uses a similar hold-to-select rule for a hand-driven cursor: the user holds still on a target for about 0.8 s and a progress ring completes the click. That work concerns gaze rather than the hand, and a suitable dwell time for hand pointing in a vocabulary app has not been measured in this project.

Resilient Dependence on Online Services

Nygard describes the circuit breaker, which stops calls to a failing service for a period and then tests whether it has recovered [11]. RFC 5861 defines a stale-if-error cache extension that lets a cache serve an expired response when an error occurs [12]. Motionary applies both ideas to dictionary lookups, together with a SQLite cache. Its online sources, the Free Dictionary API [13] and Datamuse [14], are free and keyless, so outage handling has to come from the application itself.

Game Elements in Learning Tools

Deterding et al. define gamification as the use of game design elements in non-game contexts [15]. Word Catcher uses such elements, namely rounds, a score, a timer, and lives, inside a learning app. Whether it improves vocabulary retention has not been measured in this project.

Synthesis

The sources above address event-driven design, hand tracking, dwell selection, outage handling, and game elements separately. Motionary combines them in one student-facing web app. This paper does not claim that the combination is unprecedented.

Section III Methodology ▾

Research Design

The study follows a developmental (software engineering) design: the team defined objectives, designed the architecture, implemented the system, and verified it with automated and manual checks. Motionary was developed by Group 14 for the ITC C301 Integrative Programming course (BSIT – 301i). The project documentation records its status as complete, with all planned features implemented and verified. This paper reports no user study and no data collected from human participants.

System Architecture and Technology Stack

Motionary is a single-page web app backed by a local API server. Table I lists the stack. The front end uses plain CSS design tokens with no UI framework, and fonts are Tai Heritage Pro for headings and Inter for UI and body text. The database is embedded SQLite in write-ahead logging mode [16], accessed with parameterized queries and no external database server.

Table I — Technology Stack
Layer Technology
FrontendReact 19, React Router 7; single-page app with plain CSS design tokens
BackendNode.js 26, Express 5; API on port 3001, with /api requests forwarded by Vite
Databasenode:sqlite (built into Node), WAL mode; embedded SQLite
Gesture engineGoogle MediaPipe Tasks Vision; hand landmarker on the device using WebAssembly and GPU acceleration
Online word sourcesFree Dictionary API, Datamuse; free and keyless, called only from the server
Tooling and testingVite 8, Oxlint, Vitest 3

Content and API

The database holds curated JRU vocabulary (30 words), 15 slang terms, 8 grammar topics, and the word pools used by Word Catcher, all written in original wording. The seed script can be run repeatedly without creating duplicates. Pages read this content through endpoints for health checks (/api/health), word suggestions, full dictionary entries, thesaurus data, the Word of the Day and a random word, slang, grammar, and Word Catcher games (/api/games/word-catcher).

Word Lookup and Reliability

A dictionary search passes through three tiers, and the browser never contacts the online services directly; every request goes through the Motionary server. First, the local database supplies curated words with examples and usage notes. Second, any other English word is looked up in the Free Dictionary API for definitions, phonetics, audio, and examples. Third, if that API fails, Datamuse supplies a basic definition so the user still gets an answer. Datamuse also powers search suggestions and the Thesaurus mode.

Four mechanisms protect against outages. Found words are cached in SQLite, so repeat lookups call no online service, and clean “not found” results are cached too. A circuit breaker stops calling a broken service for a short time after repeated failures and then sends one test request. Stale-if-error serves an expired cache entry when every service fails. Each result page labels its source and links to it.

Event-Driven Gesture Pipeline

Fig. 1 shows the six stages. The camera session requests the webcam and moves through four states: idle, starting, live, and error. The camera never starts by itself; the user must press “Enable camera” and allow the browser permission. In the detect stage, each video frame produces 21 landmarks per hand, and the engine counts the extended fingers and tracks the hand center and fingertip. In the stabilize stage, a pose must hold for about 150 ms to count, the cursor is smoothed, and a cooldown follows each gesture (about 1.5 s for finger poses and swipes, and 2.5 s for an open palm). Recognized gestures are published to subscribers on an event bus, and a navigation handler turns them into page changes. React Router then changes the page, and in hands-free mode a cursor overlay moves, selects by dwell, and scrolls. All video is processed on the user’s device and is never uploaded.

Interaction Modes

Motionary has three ways to navigate. Standard navigation (mouse, touch, and keyboard) is always available. Hands-free off is the default once the camera is live, and each hand pose is a shortcut to a page. Hands-free on is opt-in: it can be turned on only while the camera is live, with the toggle beside the camera icon or the H key, and it turns the hand into a pointer. Table II gives the gesture mappings. In hands-free on mode, a gold cursor follows the index fingertip, and holding still on a target for about 0.8 s completes a click. Two fingers scroll when the cursor enters the top or bottom edge zone (the outer 18% of the screen). A closed fist moved sideways swipes to the next or previous main page, and an open palm held for about 0.7 s returns home. Three and four fingers are disabled in this mode so that they cannot trigger accidental page jumps. On the landing page, an on-screen gesture keyboard lets the user type a search by dwelling on keys. A PiP window keeps showing the camera and the recognized gesture on other pages; it can be dragged, snaps to a corner, can be minimized, and its X button stops the camera.

Table II — Gesture Mappings
Gesture Hands-free off Hands-free on
1 fingerGames & QuizzesCursor; hold still to click
2 fingersWord of the DayScroll (top and bottom edge zones)
3 fingersGrammarDisabled
4 fingersSlangDisabled
FistHomeSwipe: closed fist moved sideways goes to the next or previous page
Open palmCamera pageHome (hold about 0.7 s)

Hands-free mode can be exited with the Exit hands-free button, the toggle, the Escape key, by stopping the camera or a camera error, or automatically after 60 s with no hand detected. After exiting, the normal gestures work again immediately.

Verification Procedure

Verification used four checks: automated tests with Vitest 3, static analysis with Oxlint, a production build with Vite 8, and manual and CSS accessibility checks covering color contrast, visible keyboard focus, and reduced-motion support. Privacy is handled by design, with video processed on the device. To make the contrast check reproducible, the contrast ratio of each documented color pair was also calculated with the WCAG formula [17]:

CR = (L1 + 0.05) / (L2 + 0.05) (1)

where L1 and L2 are the relative luminances of the lighter and darker colors, computed as 0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B from linearized sRGB values.

Section IV Results and Discussion ▾

System Features

Search. The search page offers Dictionary and Thesaurus modes. A dictionary entry shows the headword, a respelling (and IPA when available), a speaker button, and a Save star. Meanings are grouped by part of speech with examples, and every word inside a definition is clickable and starts a new search. Thesaurus mode lists synonyms and antonyms by part of speech, plus broader, narrower, and related words. When a word is missing, the page says so and offers clickable suggestions. Typing in the search bar shows suggestions, and focusing the empty bar shows recent and saved searches.

Learning pages. The Word of the Day page shows the word, its part of speech, pronunciation, definition, and an example sentence, and the word is chosen from the database by date, so everyone sees the same word on the same day. The Grammar and Slang pages show short topics or terms, such as “Could Of vs. Could Have” and “doomscroll,” and a “Show another” button loads a different one.

Word Catcher. A clue with a part-of-speech label and a short definition appears while words fall down the screen, and the player moves a basket to catch the one word that answers the clue (Fig. 2). A game has five rounds with five catches each. The speed choices are Relaxed (5 lives, slower), Normal (3 lives, classic), and Fast (3 lives, quicker). Only one falling word is correct, and the others are decoys picked at random from a large word pool. A wrong catch costs a life. Controls are hand position through the camera, mouse, touch, or the arrow keys (A and D also work).

Gesture camera. The camera page is the control center for gestures. It has idle, starting, error, and live states; in the live state it shows a mirrored camera view, a pill with the recognized pose, and a card listing each gesture and its destination.

Verification Results

Table III summarizes the checks. All 162 automated tests in 19 test files passed, the static analysis of 76 files found 0 errors and 0 warnings, and the production build succeeded. The accessibility checks and the privacy design are recorded as completed; they are not quantified beyond the contrast ratios in Section IV-C.

Accessibility and Design System

The design tokens are navy (#002765), yellow (#f8d834), gold (#e3b009), gold text (#8a6500), pale lime (#e9f6be), and off-white (#f5f6f8). Table IV gives the contrast ratios of the pairs whose use is documented. WCAG 2.2 requires at least 4.5:1 for normal-size text at Level AA [17], and all three pairs exceed it. The lighter gold accent (#e3b009) reaches only 1.85:1 on off-white, which fits the project’s choice to use it for accents, borders, and focus glows and to use the darker #8a6500 for gold text.

Summary of Findings

Four findings follow from the evidence, each tied to the objectives in Section I. First, the learning content and game features of objective (i) are implemented and verified, with a curated database of 30 words, 15 slang terms, and 8 grammar topics. Second, objective (ii) is met in design: the MediaPipe hand landmarker runs on the device with WebAssembly and GPU acceleration, and video is never uploaded. Third, objective (iii) is met by keeping standard navigation always available, leaving hands-free off by default, and offering several ways out of hands-free mode. Fourth, objective (iv) is supported by documented design tokens whose text pairs meet the 4.5:1 ratio. The reliability need is addressed by the three-tier lookup with caching, a circuit breaker, and stale-if-error.

These results apply patterns from the literature rather than testing them. The hold-to-select cursor follows the dwell-time idea [10], the lookup service follows the circuit breaker and stale-if-error ideas [11], [12], and the event bus follows the Observer pattern [3].

Limitations

This study has clear limits. No user study was conducted, so there are no usability scores such as the System Usability Scale [18]. Gesture recognition accuracy, end-to-end latency, and frame rate were not measured, and passing tests show that the code behaves as specified, not that gestures are recognized accurately for every user. The timing values (150 ms hold, 0.8 s dwell, 0.7 s palm hold, cooldowns, and the 60 s automatic exit) are design parameters whose suitability for different users has not been evaluated. No comparison with other dictionary apps or with a request–response baseline was made, learning outcomes were not measured, browser and device compatibility testing is not reported, and the curated database is small (30 words), so most lookups depend on the online fallbacks. The contrast computation covers only three documented pairs, not focus indicators or every combination on screen.

Research Implications

  • Theoretical. The design shows how the Observer pattern [3] can separate a noisy sensing stage from the user interface: because stabilization happens before dispatch, subscribers receive discrete gesture events. This paper does not test whether the decoupling improves maintainability.
  • Practical. Developers of education web apps can reuse the approach of stabilizing poses before dispatch, keeping standard input always available, making the camera opt-in, and processing video on the device.
  • Societal. Motionary relates to SDG 4 (Quality Education) [5] by offering vocabulary, grammar, and slang learning with an optional touchless input route. Whether the touchless route benefits particular groups of learners has not been studied.
Section V Conclusion & Recommendations ▾

Conclusion

Motionary is a student encyclopedia web app for JRU that adds optional, on-device hand-gesture navigation to a dictionary, thesaurus, Word of the Day, grammar guides, slang catalog, and the Word Catcher game. Its event-driven pipeline captures video, detects hand landmarks, stabilizes poses, and publishes gestures to subscribers through an event bus. Standard input always works alongside gestures. The project documentation reports all planned features as implemented and verified, with 162 passing tests, a clean static analysis of 76 files, and a successful production build. The work does not yet measure gesture accuracy, latency, usability, or learning outcomes.

Recommendations

For future work, the authors recommend:

  1. a usability study with JRU students, for example with the System Usability Scale [18];
  2. measurements of gesture recognition accuracy and end-to-end latency across cameras and lighting conditions;
  3. an evaluation of the dwell time and cooldown values with different users;
  4. a study of whether Word Catcher improves vocabulary retention;
  5. a larger curated vocabulary, so that fewer lookups rely on the online fallbacks; and
  6. a broader accessibility audit, including focus-indicator contrast [17].
